questions.learningObjective: Understand parametric curve as traced by parameter
questions.stem: In a historical case, a parametric curve is best described as?

options.text: A set of points (x(t),y(t)) as t varies

questions.explanation: Parametric curve consists of points (x(t),y(t)) traced as parameter t varies over an interval.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Eliminate parameter to get Cartesian equation
questions.stem: In a historical case, x=cos t, y=sin t. Eliminate t: x^2+y^2=?
questions.explanation: Squaring and adding removes the parameter: x^2 + y^2 = cos^2 t + sin^2 t = 1, the unit circle. The key step is keeping the Pythagorean identity, since dropping either square would not cancel t.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Recognize domain restriction lost when eliminating parameter
questions.stem: In a historical case, eliminating t may lose information about?

options.text: The interval of t and direction of motion

options.misconception: treats dimension as the lost information, although dimension is preserved

questions.explanation: A Cartesian equation records which points lie on a curve but not when or in which direction they are traversed. Elimination can discard the interval of t and the orientation, so quite different motions can share one equation.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, x=t^2, y=t^3. dy/dx at t=2?
questions.explanation: For parametric curves dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 3t^2/(2t) = 3t/2 when t is nonzero. At t = 2 this is 3; substituting into dy/dt alone would give 12 and ignore the horizontal rate.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, horizontal tangent to parametric curve occurs when?

options.misconception: thinks slope 1 signals horizontal, but horizontal means slope 0

questions.explanation: Since dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), a horizontal tangent needs numerator dy/dt = 0 with denominator dx/dt nonzero. If both vanish the curve may have a cusp, while dx/dt = 0 with dy/dt nonzero produces a vertical tangent.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Interpret zero velocity in parametric motion
questions.stem: In a historical case, zero velocity r'(t)=0 means the particle?

options.misconception: assumes zero velocity forces infinite acceleration, which does not follow

questions.explanation: The velocity vector r'(t) is the instantaneous rate of change of position; if it is the zero vector, every coordinate has zero rate and the particle is momentarily at rest. That does not force a straight path, unit speed, or infinite acceleration.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Compute speed as magnitude of velocity
questions.stem: In a historical case, r(t)=<t,2t>. Speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is the magnitude of velocity: r'(t) = <1,2>, so speed = sqrt(1^2 + 2^2) = sqrt(5), about 2.236. It is constant here because the velocity components are constant.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, x=t, y=t^2. d2y/dx2?
questions.explanation: First dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 2t/1 = 2t. Then d^2y/dx^2 = [d/dt(dy/dx)]/(dx/dt) = 2/1 = 2; differentiating with respect to t alone forgets to divide by dx/dt.
questions.hint: Differentiate dy/dx w.r.t. t then divide by dx/dt.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.topic: Tangent line to a parametric curve
questions.learningObjective: Write tangent line at a point
questions.stem: In a historical case, tangent line to parametric curve uses point (x(t0),y(t0)) and slope?

options.misconception: uses dx/dy, the reciprocal of the required slope

questions.explanation: A tangent line uses the point (x(t0), y(t0)) and the slope dy/dx at t0, namely (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Using dx/dy inverts the slope, while dy/dt alone ignores the horizontal rate.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify region traced by parametric equations
questions.stem: In a historical case, x=cos t, y=sin t, 0<=t<=pi traces?

options.misconception: uses the lower semicircle, implying y is negative on [0,pi]

questions.explanation: With x = cos t and y = sin t, y is nonnegative on [0,pi], so the path is the upper semicircle traced from (1,0) to (-1,0). Restricting to [0,pi/2] gives a quarter circle and ignoring the interval gives the full circle.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, x(t)=sin t on [0,pi/2]. Largest x?
questions.explanation: sin t increases from 0 to 1 on [0,pi/2], so its largest value is 1 at t = pi/2. Checking endpoints and interior critical points is the standard way to maximize on a closed interval.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, a sharper bend has?

options.misconception: treats a sharp bend as having no definable curvature

questions.explanation: Curvature is the rate at which tangent direction turns per unit arc length, so a sharper bend has larger curvature. A straight line has curvature zero, and a cusp is not a small-curvature case.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Know curvature of straight line is zero
questions.stem: In a historical case, curvature of a straight line is?

options.misconception: claims a straight line has undefined curvature, but the bend rate is exactly zero

questions.explanation: Curvature is 1/r for a circle, and a straight line behaves like a circle of infinite radius, so its curvature is 0. Values such as 1 or infinity come from confusing it with a unit circle or a cusp.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Compare curvature at vertex vs elsewhere
questions.stem: In a historical case, for y=x^2, curvature is largest at?

options.misconception: picks x = 1 with no relation to where the denominator is smallest
claims a parabola has no point of largest curvature, though it does

questions.explanation: For y = f(x) curvature is |f''|/(1 + (f')^2)^(3/2); for f = x^2 it is 2/(1 + 4x^2)^(3/2), largest at x = 0. Away from the vertex the growing slope reduces the curvature.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Know curvature of circle radius r is 1/r
questions.stem: In a historical case, circle radius 4. Curvature?
questions.explanation: For a circle, curvature is the reciprocal of the radius, so kappa = 1/4 = 0.25. A larger radius bends more gently, which is why curvature decreases as r grows.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Convert Cartesian point to polar radius
questions.stem: In a historical case, Cartesian point (3,4). Polar radius r?
questions.explanation: The polar radius is distance from the origin, r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5. This is the 3-4-5 triangle; adding before squaring would wrongly give 7.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, polar (r=2, theta=pi/3). x-coordinate?
questions.explanation: Conversion uses x = r cos(theta), so x = 2*cos(pi/3) = 2*(1/2) = 1. Using sine instead would give the y-coordinate rather than x.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, area of rose r=a cos(n theta) uses?

options.misconception: uses the integral of r^2 with the essential factor 1/2 omitted

questions.explanation: Polar area uses (1/2) times the integral of r^2 dtheta; the 1/2 comes from the triangular area element and r must be squared. For a rose, integrate over the interval tracing one petal and account for the petal count.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, polar arc length integrand includes?

options.misconception: uses r alone, ignoring the radial rate of change
uses dr/dtheta alone, dropping the radius term

questions.explanation: A polar arc length element is sqrt(r^2 + (dr/dtheta)^2) dtheta, combining radial and angular motion by the Pythagorean theorem. Using r alone ignores how the radius changes, while using only dr/dtheta ignores the radius.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, area inside limaçon r=a+b cosθ (a>b>0) is?
questions.explanation: For a > b > 0 the limacon r = a + b cos(theta) is traced once as theta runs from 0 to 2pi, so its area is (1/2) times the integral of r^2 over that full interval. Integrating only to pi covers half the curve, and dropping the square gives a length-like quantity.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Compute arc length element for spiral
questions.stem: In a historical case, spiral r=θ. Arc length element sqrt(r^2+(dr/dθ)^2) = ? at θ=1
questions.explanation: For r = theta, dr/dtheta = 1, so the arc element sqrt(r^2 + (dr/dtheta)^2) is sqrt(theta^2 + 1); at theta = 1 this is sqrt(2), about 1.414. Omitting the derivative term would give just 1.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, negative r in polar coordinates means?

options.misconception: treats a negative radius as putting the point at the origin

options.text: Plot in opposite direction of θ

questions.explanation: A negative polar radius plots the point pi radians from the ray at angle theta, that is at (|r|, theta + pi). It is a legitimate plotted point, not the origin, and the sign belongs to r rather than to theta.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, (1,2)+(3,4) x-component?
questions.explanation: Vectors add componentwise, so (1,2) + (3,4) = (1+3, 2+4) = (4,6) and the x-component is 4. Adding only one vector's coordinates misses the other vector entirely.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, vector <3,4>. Unit vector magnitude?
questions.explanation: A unit vector has magnitude 1 by definition; normalizing <3,4> gives <3/5,4/5>, whose length is 1. The length 5 belongs to the original vector, not its unit version.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Write parametric line through point with direction
questions.stem: In a historical case, line through (1,2) direction <3,4>: x(t)=1+3t. At t=1, x?
questions.explanation: Substituting t = 1 into x(t) = 1 + 3t gives x = 1 + 3 = 4. The parameter scales the direction <3,4>, so t = 1 moves one full direction step from the base point.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Recall arc length formula for y=f(x)
questions.stem: In a historical case, arc length of y=f(x) from a to b is ∫ sqrt(1+?) dx?

options.misconception: uses 1 + f(x), mixing the function value into a slope-based formula

questions.explanation: Arc length of y = f(x) is the integral of sqrt(1 + (f'(x))^2) dx; the 1 and the squared derivative come from the Pythagorean theorem on an infinitesimal segment. Using f'(x) unsquared or f(x)^2 are common errors.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Recall area formula under parametric curve
questions.stem: In a historical case, area under parametric curve x=x(t), y=y(t) is ∫?

options.misconception: integrates y(t) dt without converting dx into x'(t) dt
integrates x(t) dt, which does not represent area under the curve

questions.explanation: Area under a parametric curve is the integral of y(t) x'(t) dt, because y times dx replaces the y dx of rectangular area. Using y alone omits the dx conversion, while x times y' swaps the roles of the variables.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Recall Jacobian for polar double integral
questions.stem: In a historical case, double integral in polar adds factor?

options.misconception: uses 1/r instead of the Jacobian factor r

questions.explanation: In polar coordinates the area element is dA = r dr dtheta; the extra factor r is the Jacobian of the transformation. Omitting it incorrectly treats polar cells as if they were rectangular.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, polar point (r=4, θ=π/6). y-coordinate?
questions.explanation: Conversion uses y = r sin(theta), so y = 4*sin(pi/6) = 4*(1/2) = 2. Using cosine here would produce the x-coordinate instead of y.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.topic: Distance from the origin to a line
questions.learningObjective: Compute distance from origin to line
questions.stem: In a historical case, line 3x+4y=0
questions.explanation: The distance from a point to a line ax + by + c = 0 is |a x0 + b y0 + c| divided by sqrt(a^2 + b^2); the denominator normalizes by the length of the coefficient vector. Substituting the line's coefficients and the point's coordinates gives the distance.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, dx/dt=3, dy/dt=4. Speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is sqrt((dx/dt)^2 + (dy/dt)^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5. As the magnitude of velocity it does not depend on the signs of the components.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, polar area of sector radius 2 angle π/2?
questions.explanation: A polar sector has area (1/2) r^2 theta, so here (1/2)*4*(pi/2) = pi, about 3.1416. Using the full circle area pi r^2 would ignore the sector's fraction of a full turn.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Handle signed radius in polar plot
questions.stem: In a historical case, point (-2, π/4) in polar is equivalent to?

options.misconception: adds pi to the angle but leaves r negative, reversing the point
uses -pi/4, which is not the antipodal direction of pi/4

questions.explanation: A negative radius is converted by adding pi to the angle and flipping the sign: (-2, pi/4) = (2, pi/4 + pi) = (2, 5pi/4). Keeping r negative at 5pi/4 would point in the opposite direction again.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.topic: Where the polar area factor comes from
questions.learningObjective: Explain origin of factor 1/2 in polar area
questions.stem: In a historical case, why is there a 1/2 in polar area formula?

answer.exemplar: The area of a circular sector is half r squared theta, and summing infinitesimal sectors gives the one half factor in the integral.

questions.explanation: Polar area sums infinitesimal sectors whose area is (1/2)r^2 dθ, yielding the 1/2 factor.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, what can elimination of a parameter not record?

answer.exemplar: Elimination cannot record the direction of motion or the specific interval of the parameter values that produced the curve.

questions.explanation: Elimination loses the parameter's interval and the direction in which the curve is traced.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, why does zero velocity not mean the path stops forever?

answer.exemplar: Zero velocity at an instant means the particle is momentarily at rest, but it may accelerate and move again afterward.

questions.explanation: Zero velocity at an instant is momentary; acceleration can restart motion.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Explain why speed is magnitude of velocity
questions.stem: In a historical case, why is speed the magnitude of velocity?

answer.exemplar: Speed measures how fast position changes regardless of direction, so it is the magnitude of the velocity vector.

questions.explanation: Speed is scalar rate of change of position, hence magnitude of velocity vector.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Explain sign ambiguity in polar coordinates
questions.stem: In a historical case, why do polar coordinates have sign ambiguity?

answer.exemplar: The same point can be represented by (r,θ) and (-r,θ+π), so representation is not unique.

questions.explanation: A point has multiple polar representations due to negative r and angle shifts.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, rose r=cos(3θ) has how many petals?

options.misconception: gives 2 petals, which would require n = 1 or a different curve

questions.explanation: For r = a cos(n theta), an odd n gives n petals and an even n gives 2n. Here n = 3 is odd, so the rose has 3 petals; doubling to 6 applies only to even n.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, limacon r=a+b cosθ with a<b has?

options.misconception: describes the circle obtained when b = 0, not the a < b case
describes the dimpled limacon that occurs when a > b
describes the convex limacon, which has no inner loop

questions.explanation: For r = a + b cos(theta) an inner loop appears exactly when a < b, because r becomes negative over part of the interval. When a = b the curve is a cardioid, and a > b gives a dimpled or convex limacon with no loop.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, stage 1: a parametric curve uses parameter t; stage 2: Cartesian uses x as independent. Which is more general?

options.misconception: claims the Cartesian form is more general, reversing the comparison
claims neither form is more general, ignoring curves that fail the vertical line test

questions.explanation: Parametric equations can describe loops, vertical tangents, and curves that fail the vertical line test, which a function y = f(x) cannot. Cartesian form is the special case obtained by taking x as the parameter.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, x=2t+1, y=3t-2. Eliminate t: at x=5, y?
questions.explanation: From x = 2t + 1 we get t = (x-1)/2. Substituting gives y = 3(x-1)/2 - 2; at x = 5, t = 2 and y = 4. Eliminating t first is cleaner than guessing a value of t.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, student eliminates t from x=cos t,y=sin t and claims full circle traced once. Find error.

options.misconception: claims elimination is always wrong, whereas the equation it yields is correct

options.text: Elimination loses interval; t range may trace only part

options.misconception: claims no information is lost, ignoring the lost interval and orientation

questions.explanation: Eliminating t gives the correct Cartesian equation but cannot tell which part of the circle is traced or how often. The parameter range must be kept separately, so claiming no information is lost is the error.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, x=t^2, y=t^3. Slope at t=1?
questions.explanation: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 3t^2/(2t) = 3t/2 for nonzero t, so at t = 1 the slope is 1.5. Using dy/dt alone would give 3 and ignore the horizontal rate.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, x=t, y=t^3-3t. Horizontal tangent when dy/dt=0: t values? Smallest positive?
questions.explanation: Horizontal tangents occur where dy/dt = 0 and dx/dt is nonzero. Here dy/dt = 3t^2 - 3, so t = plus or minus 1 and the smallest positive value is 1.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, r(t)=<t^2-1, t>. Velocity zero when? t value?
questions.explanation: Velocity is the componentwise derivative of the position vector, and the particle is at rest when every component of r'(t) is zero. Setting each component to zero and solving for t identifies the instant of rest.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, r(t)=<cos t, sin t, t>. Speed?
questions.explanation: r'= <-sin t, cos t, 1>, speed = sqrt(sin^2+cos^2+1)=sqrt2≈1.414.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, x=t, y=t^3. d2y/dx2 at t=2?
questions.explanation: First dy/dx = 3t^2/1 = 3t^2. Then d^2y/dx^2 = [d/dt(3t^2)]/(dx/dt) = 6t/1 = 6t, which is 12 at t = 2. Dividing by dx/dt at the second stage is the step most often omitted.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.topic: Tangent line to a parametric curve
questions.stem: In a historical case, x=t^2, y=t^3 at t=1. Tangent slope dy/dx?
questions.explanation: The slope is dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 3t^2/(2t) = 3t/2, so at t = 1 it is 1.5. This is the ordinary parametric slope rule, not a separate formula for tangent lines.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, x=cos t, y=sin t, 0<=t<=π/2 traces?

options.misconception: uses the lower quarter, implying y is negative on this interval

questions.explanation: For t in [0,pi/2] both cos t and sin t are nonnegative, so the path is the quarter circle in QI from (1,0) to (0,1). Extending the interval to [0,pi] would give a semicircle instead.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, y(t)=sin t on [0,π]. Largest y?
questions.explanation: sin t rises to 1 at t = pi/2 and falls back to 0 at t = pi, so its maximum is 1. Checking the interior critical point as well as the endpoints is essential.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, circle radius 2. Curvature?
questions.explanation: Curvature of a circle is 1/r, so for radius 2 it is 1/2 = 0.5. Smaller circles have larger curvature because the tangent turns faster per unit length.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, Cartesian (-3,-4). Polar radius?
questions.explanation: Radius is distance from the origin, r = sqrt((-3)^2 + (-4)^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5. Negative coordinates do not make r negative; the angle carries the directional information.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, polar (r=5, θ=π/2). y-coordinate?
questions.explanation: y = r sin(theta) = 5*sin(pi/2) = 5*1 = 5. At pi/2 the ray points straight up, so all of r contributes to the y-coordinate.
questions.subject: CALCULUS_II

provenance.author: bank-team-calculus-2
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: In a historical case, rose r=cos(4θ) has how many petals?

options.misconception: uses n for even n (should be 2n)
gives 2 petals, not the 2n required for an even n

questions.explanation: For r = a cos(n theta), an even n produces 2n petals, so n = 4 gives 8 petals. The odd-n rule would give only 4 petals and does not apply here.

questions.stem: In a historical case, r=2 constant. Arc length element sqrt(r^2+(dr/dθ)^2)?
questions.explanation: With r = 2 constant, dr/dtheta = 0, so the element sqrt(r^2 + (dr/dtheta)^2) is sqrt(4 + 0) = 2. A constant radius traces a circle whose arc element is simply r dtheta.

questions.stem: In a historical case, limacon r=a+a cosθ (a>0) is a?

options.misconception: describes the convex limacon, which needs a at least 2b
describes the inner-loop limacon, which needs a < b rather than a = b
describes the circle obtained when b is zero

questions.explanation: When a = b in r = a + b cos(theta), the inner loop shrinks to a cusp at the origin and the curve is a cardioid. Cases a > b and a < b give a dimpled limacon and a limacon with an inner loop respectively.

questions.learningObjective: Compute spiral arc length element at θ=0
questions.stem: In a historical case, spiral r=θ. Arc length element at θ=0?
questions.explanation: For r = theta, dr/dtheta = 1, so the element is sqrt(theta^2 + 1); at theta = 0 it equals 1. The derivative term keeps the element from vanishing at the origin.

questions.stem: In a historical case, point (-1, 0) in polar lies where?

options.misconception: places a negative radius at angle 0 on the positive y-axis
treats the negative radius as placing the point at the origin

questions.explanation: The point (-1,0) in polar means r = -1 at angle 0, which plots one unit opposite the ray at 0, i.e. at (1,pi) on the negative x-axis. A negative radius is neither the origin nor a point on the positive axis.

questions.stem: In a historical case, (3,4)+(-3,-4) magnitude?
questions.explanation: Componentwise addition gives (0,0), whose magnitude is 0. The two vectors are exact opposites and cancel; adding their magnitudes would incorrectly give 10.
